title: Hosea's Marriage and the Children of Judgment
summary: God tells Hosea to marry a woman who will be unfaithful, because Israel has been unfaithful to the LORD. Hosea marries Gomer, and the names God gives their three children announce judgment on the northern kingdom: Jezreel, Lo-ruhamah (No Compassion), and Lo-ammi (Not My People). Yet the chapter ends by reversing those names, promising a people as numerous as the sand, called children of the living God, reunited under one leader.
story: Hosea opens the collection of twelve shorter prophetic books sometimes called the Minor Prophets, named for their length, not their importance. We are in the northern kingdom of Israel, which split from Judah and David's royal line after Solomon's death (1 Kings 12) and has worshiped the LORD at its own shrines, often mixed with the worship of Baal. God has sent prophets before, Elijah and Elisha among them, and now he makes a prophet's own household into a message. The chapter lays out the book's whole pattern in miniature: sin named, judgment announced, and then, unexpectedly, a promise that goes all the way back to God's word to Abraham about descendants like the sand of the sea (Genesis 22:17).
historical:
Verse 1 places Hosea in the eighth century BC. He began under Jeroboam II of Israel, whose long reign (roughly the first half of the eighth century BC) brought expansion and prosperity (2 Kings 14:23-29), and the list of Judean kings reaches to Hezekiah, who came to the throne in the late 720s or around 715 BC. Hosea's ministry likely ran from before Jeroboam's death, around 753 BC, into the last years of the northern kingdom, which fell to Assyria in 722 BC. That the superscription names four kings of Judah and only one of Israel may reflect the book's later preservation in Judah; it may also quietly pass over the unstable northern kings who followed Jeroboam.

The name Jezreel carries history. Jezreel was a royal city and the broad, fertile valley beside it. There, about 841 BC, the army commander Jehu, anointed at Elisha's word, killed King Joram of Israel, King Ahaziah of Judah, Queen Jezebel, and the whole house of Ahab (2 Kings 9 to 10). Jehu founded the dynasty to which Jeroboam II belonged. Though 2 Kings 10:30 credits Jehu with carrying out God's judgment on Ahab's house, Hosea announces judgment for the bloodshed of Jezreel, apparently for the brutality and self-serving excess with which it was done. Jehu's dynasty ended when Jeroboam's son Zechariah was assassinated after six months (2 Kings 15:8-12), and the kingdom itself ended some thirty years later.
cultural:
Names in the ancient Near East were often statements, and prophets sometimes gave their children names that carried a message (Isaiah's sons had names too, Isaiah 7:3; 8:3). Hosea's children became walking sermons. Anyone who asked a child's name heard a verdict on the nation. Lo-ruhamah means not pitied or no compassion; ruhamah comes from the word for the womb and the tender love of a parent. Lo-ammi, Not My People, reverses the covenant formula of Sinai, I will be your God and you will be my people (Leviticus 26:12).

The expression translated take a prostitute as your wife is literally a wife of harlotries, and the phrase children of adultery follows it. Marriage in ancient Israel was arranged between families, and a husband's honor was bound up with his wife's faithfulness. For a prophet to marry a woman known for promiscuity, or one who would become unfaithful, would have brought public shame on him. That shame is the point: God is showing what Israel's unfaithfulness has done to him. The land's prostitution means its worship of Baal, whom many Israelites credited with rain and fertile fields.
literary: The chapter is prose narrative with embedded divine speech. It follows a clear rhythm: a birth, a name given by God, and an explanation beginning with for. Each child's name is harsher than the one before, moving from punishment of a dynasty (Jezreel), to withdrawal of compassion from the nation (Lo-ruhamah), to the dissolving of the covenant itself (Lo-ammi). Then verses 10-11 turn every name inside out. Not My People becomes sons of the living God; the scattered become gathered; and Jezreel, which means God sows, changes from a place of bloodshed into a great day of planting. In many Hebrew Bibles, verses 10-11 are numbered as 2:1-2, so the promise opens the next chapter; English Bibles place it here.

outline.t: The word of the LORD to Hosea
The command to marry, and Gomer
Jezreel: the end of Jehu's house
Lo-ruhamah: no compassion for Israel, deliverance for Judah
The names reversed: children of the living God

doctrines.note: Lo-ammi, you are not My people, and I am not your God, is the covenant bond spoken in reverse. Israel's relationship with God was a covenant, like a marriage, with obligations of loyalty; breaking it has real consequences.
The chapter calls Israel's worship of other gods prostitution and adultery. Idolatry is not merely a mistaken idea about God; it is the betrayal of a relationship.
Judah will be saved not by bow or sword or war (verse 7), but by the LORD their God. Salvation is God's own act, not the product of military or political strength.
Judgment is not God's last word. In the very place where it was said, You are not My people, they will be called sons of the living God. God's promises to Abraham survive Israel's unfaithfulness.

words.note: Zanah, to commit sexual immorality or to act as a prostitute. The verb, and nouns built from it, run through Hosea as the book's central image for Israel's unfaithfulness to God. In verse 2 it appears in the wife of harlotries and in the land's flagrant prostituting of itself. Whether the phrase describes Gomer's past or what she became is debated (see the hard question).

Jezreel, God sows or may God sow. The name is double-edged: it recalls the massacre at the city of Jezreel, but its meaning points to planting and harvest. Hosea uses both senses, so that the same name announces judgment in verse 4 and a great day of restoration in verse 11 (compare 2:22-23).

Racham, to have compassion, from the same root as the word for womb. It describes the tender, protective love of a parent for a child. Lo-ruhamah, Not Pitied, is a terrible name for a daughter, and 2:23 will reverse it: I will have compassion on No Compassion.

christ: The New Testament takes up the reversal of the children's names directly. Paul quotes Hosea's promise that those called Not My People will be called children of the living God to show that God's mercy now reaches Gentiles as well as Jews (Romans 9:25-26), and Peter tells scattered believers that once they were not a people but now they are the people of God (1 Peter 2:10). Hosea was speaking of Israel's restoration after judgment; the apostles see the same pattern of mercy widening in Christ. The promise that Judah and Israel will appoint one leader (verse 11) belongs to the prophetic hope for a single king who reunites God's divided people, which Hosea soon ties to David's line (3:5). Beneath it all is the image of a faithful husband bound to an unfaithful partner, which the New Testament fulfills in Christ, who loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25).

hard.q: Did God really command a prophet to marry a prostitute?
hard.a:
The command troubles readers because it seems to require the prophet to do something shameful. Interpreters have taken it in several ways. Some hold that Gomer was already known for sexual immorality, perhaps connected with the fertility worship of the shrines, and that the command is meant to shock: God has bound himself to a people like that. Others, noting that the text never calls Gomer a prostitute directly, read the phrase as looking ahead: she was faithful when Hosea married her but would later be unfaithful, and the narrative describes her by what she became. This fits the picture of Israel, who was faithful in her youth (2:15) and strayed later. Still others, including some medieval Jewish interpreters, proposed that the marriage took place in a vision or is a parable, not an event, though most modern scholars think the specific names of Gomer and her father suggest a real marriage.

On any of these views the point is the same: Hosea's pain mirrors God's. Scripture does not present this as a model for others to imitate; it is a unique prophetic sign in which a man's life carried the grief of God. It is also worth noticing that the text says the children are children of adultery, but it names only the first son explicitly as born to Hosea (verse 3).

questions: God describes Israel's worship of other gods as adultery. How does that picture change the way you think about sin?
Each child's name carried a message. What would someone learn about your deepest loyalties from the way you live?
The chapter moves from Not My People to children of the living God. Where have you seen God bring hope out of a situation that seemed to be only judgment?
